prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val][adversarial] Feature matrix with long row headers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Capability" · longest unbreakable word 82px · one-line width 370px
  col 2: header "Free" · longest unbreakable word 32px · one-line width 32px
  col 3: header "Team" · longest unbreakable word 39px · one-line width 39px
  col 4: header "Business" · longest unbreakable word 65px · one-line width 65px
  col 5: header "Enterprise" · longest unbreakable word 75px · one-line width 75px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
This table cannot fit without splitting words at 360px. You MAY choose a total wider than 359px (the reader then scrolls horizontally), or squeeze and accept splits — a design decision.
Rendering convention: the screenshot always shows the WHOLE table. Anything beyond the dashed box is not clipped; it is the part a reader reaches by scrolling sideways, so judge both what fits in the box at first sight and the cost of scrolling to the rest.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 360px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare which subscription plans include each capability.","reading":"Readers scan capability names down the first column, then compare availability across the plan columns in the same row.","groups":["Free, Team, Business and Enterprise are parallel plan columns; consistent spacing helps readers compare them."],"keep_intact":["Plan names where space permits","SAML 2.0 and four-hour as meaningful terms","Availability marks"],"may_wrap":["Capability descriptions at word boundaries; their multiple lines can share the row height across all plan columns","Plan headers if a compact, no-scroll layout is preferred"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[200,53,60,86,96],"idea":"Give capability descriptions room to wrap naturally and keep every plan name intact, accepting horizontal scrolling to see the Enterprise column."},{"name":"B","widths":[103,53,60,65,78],"idea":"Fit the table within the viewport while keeping capability words and the first two plan names intact, accepting split Business and Enterprise headers and taller rows."},{"name":"C","widths":[160,42,45,52,60],"idea":"Favor readable capability descriptions within the viewport, accepting splits in the plan headers to keep all plan values visible together."}]}
